- **Designs.** Bunching estimators at salient thresholds (round numbers,
  quotas, tax kinks). Regression discontinuity around reference points.
  Experiments that manipulate expectations independently of outcomes, as in
  @abeler2011. Structural models that let the reference point adapt.
- **Measures.** Expected outcomes (forecasts, betting lines, guidance),
  distance from goals, past prices and wages, and self-reported reference
  points.
:::

::: {.pitfall}
**Choosing the reference point after seeing the data.** Because almost any
number can be a reference point, a study that searches for one that "works"
will usually find it. Pre-register the reference point, justify it from
institutional features or measured expectations, and show that alternative
candidates do not fit equally well.
:::

## Status Quo Bias {#status-quo-bias}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** People disproportionately choose the option that represents
the current state of affairs or the default, even when switching is cheap and
the alternatives are at least as good.

**Origins.** Economics and decision science. Named and documented by
@samuelson1988. Linked to loss aversion by @kahneman1991 and @tversky1991.

**Level of analysis.** Individual choice, with large aggregate effects in
organizations and public policy (retirement saving, insurance, organ donation,
subscriptions).

**Key constructs.** Status quo, default option, loss aversion, inertia,
transaction and switching costs, regret, implied endorsement.

**Boundary conditions.** Weaker when the status quo is clearly inferior,
when active choice is required, when decision makers are expert or highly
motivated, and when switching is made salient and easy.

**Related theories.** [Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect)),
[Choice architecture](#choice-architecture) (Section \@ref(choice-architecture)),
[Loss aversion](#loss-aversion),
[Escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment) (Section \@ref(escalation-of-commitment)).
:::

### Core logic and evidence

@samuelson1988 presented participants with hypothetical decision problems,
such as how to invest an inheritance, in two versions. In the neutral version,
all options were presented on an equal footing. In the status quo version, one
option was described as the current state of affairs. Options were chosen
substantially more often when they were designated as the status quo. The
authors then showed the same pattern in field data: in employee health plans and
in retirement allocations, people rarely revisited choices they had made years
earlier, even as their circumstances and the options changed.

Loss aversion offers a natural explanation [@kahneman1991]. If the status quo
is the reference point, then every alternative involves giving up some features
of the current option (losses) in exchange for others (gains). Because the
losses loom larger, the current option wins unless the alternative is clearly
better. But status quo bias is overdetermined. Table \@ref(tab:pt-tab-sqb)
lists the main explanations and the evidence that would distinguish among
them, and Figure \@ref(fig:pt-fig-sqb) shows how they combine.

```{r pt-tab-sqb}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Explanation, ~Mechanism, ~`Distinguishing prediction`,
  "Loss aversion", "Departures from the reference point are coded as losses on some attributes", "Bias larger when alternatives trade off attributes (some better, some worse)",
  "Inertia and procrastination", "Acting requires effort and attention that people postpone", "Bias shrinks when active choice is required or switching is made effortless",
  "Transaction and search costs", "Switching has real costs", "Bias scales with the cost of switching",
  "Implied endorsement", "Defaults are read as advice from the choice architect", "Bias larger when the default setter is trusted and the decision maker is uncertain",
  "Anticipated regret", "Bad outcomes after switching feel worse than after staying", "Bias larger when outcomes will be observed and attributed to the choice",
  "Psychological inertia", "A general preference for not acting without a compelling reason", "Bias appears even when no losses are involved (Gal, 2006)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Explanations for status quo bias.")
```

```{r pt-fig-sqb, fig.cap = "Multiple pathways to status quo bias. Loss aversion is one route among several, and choice architects can intervene at each one (active choice, simplified switching, careful selection of defaults)."}
mechanism_diagram(sprintf('
  SQ [label = "Status quo\\nor default option", %s]
  LA [label = "Loss aversion\\n(alternatives coded\\nas losses)", %s]
  IN [label = "Inertia and\\nprocrastination", %s]
  TC [label = "Switching and\\nsearch costs", %s]
  EN [label = "Implied\\nendorsement", %s]
  RG [label = "Anticipated\\nregret", %s]
  B  [label = "Status quo bias\\n(default retained)", %s]
  AC [label = "Active choice,\\neasy switching,\\nsalient reminders", %s]
  SQ -> LA -> B
  SQ -> IN -> B
  SQ -> TC -> B
  SQ -> EN -> B
  SQ -> RG -> B
  AC -> B [style = dashed, label = " weakens"]
', node_construct, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_mechanism, node_outcome, node_moderator), height = 400)
```

**Insurance framing.** @johnson1993 documented a natural experiment in
automobile insurance. Around 1990, New Jersey and Pennsylvania both
offered drivers a choice between a cheaper policy that limited the right to sue
for pain and suffering and a more expensive policy that preserved the full right
to sue. In New Jersey, the default was the limited policy. In Pennsylvania, the
default was the full policy. In each state, most drivers ended up with their
state's default, so that two economically similar populations held very
different coverage. The same paper reported laboratory evidence that insurance
choices violate basic laws of probability. In one study, people were willing to
pay more for flight insurance covering death from terrorism than for insurance
covering death from any cause, which necessarily includes terrorism.

**Retirement saving.** @madrian2001 studied a large US firm that changed its
401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment for new employees. Participation
rose sharply, from about 37% to 86% among employees with comparable tenure.
Many automatically enrolled employees also kept both the default contribution
rate (3% of pay) and the default investment (a money market fund), even though
few employees hired before the change had chosen that combination. The authors
attributed the effect to inertia and to employees' perception of the default as
investment advice. The study helped launch the modern policy interest in
defaults, discussed in [Choice architecture](#choice-architecture) (Section \@ref(choice-architecture)), and
inspired *Save More Tomorrow*, which asks employees to commit in advance to
raising their saving rate out of future pay increases, so that saving more
never requires a cut in take-home pay that would be coded as a loss
[@thaler2004].

::: {.business-case}
**401(k) auto-enrollment.** Automatic enrollment converts status quo bias from
an obstacle into a lever. The design lessons from @madrian2001 and
@thaler2004 are now standard practice. (1) Make participation the default.
(2) Choose the default contribution rate and fund carefully, because many
employees will keep them, so a low default rate can reduce saving for
employees who would otherwise have chosen more. (3) Use automatic escalation
tied to pay increases, so that higher contributions are never experienced as
a loss of take-home pay. (4) Preserve easy opt-out, which keeps the policy
libertarian and protects employees for whom the default is wrong. The same
logic underlies auto-renewal of subscriptions, but there the firm, not the
customer, benefits from inertia, which is why regulators increasingly require
easy cancellation.
:::

::: {.business-case}
**Free trials and the reference point.** A free trial combines three
prospect-theory mechanisms. During the trial the customer acquires a sense of
ownership, so cancelling is coded as giving up something already possessed
([Endowment effect](#endowment-effect) (Section \@ref(endowment-effect))). If the trial converts automatically
into a paid subscription, continuing becomes the status quo. And the first
payment, which arrives after the customer has adapted to having the service,
may be evaluated against a reference point of zero cost. **Illustrative
scenario:** a streaming service comparing an opt-in trial (customers must
actively subscribe at the end) with an opt-out trial (customers are charged
unless they cancel) should expect higher conversion under opt-out, but also more
complaints, chargebacks, and regulatory risk, and lower retention among
customers who converted only through inertia.
:::

## Myopic Loss Aversion {#myopic-loss-aversion}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Investors who are loss averse and who evaluate their portfolios
frequently will find risky assets unattractive, because frequent evaluation
reveals many short-run losses. The combination, *myopic loss aversion*, can
explain why stocks must offer a large premium over bonds to be held.

**Origins.** Finance and behavioural economics. @benartzi1995, motivated by the
equity premium puzzle of @mehra1985. Experimental tests in @gneezy1997 and
@thaler1997.

**Level of analysis.** Individual investors, with implications for asset prices
and for the design of pension plans and investment platforms.

**Key constructs.** Loss aversion, evaluation period, narrow framing (choice
bracketing), equity premium, feedback frequency.

**Boundary conditions.** Requires that gains and losses be evaluated over short
horizons and in isolation from other wealth. Weaker when investors can commit
to long horizons or receive aggregated feedback.

**Related theories.** [Loss aversion](#loss-aversion),
[Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance) (Section \@ref(behavioral-finance)),
[Portfolio theory](#portfolio-theory) (Section \@ref(portfolio-theory)).
:::

### The equity premium puzzle

Over long periods, US stocks have earned far higher average returns than
short-term government bonds. @mehra1985 showed that standard
consumption-based asset pricing models with plausible levels of risk aversion
can account for only a small fraction of the historical premium: matching it
requires a degree of risk aversion that seems implausibly high. This is the
**equity premium puzzle**.

@benartzi1995 offered a behavioural explanation built from two ingredients.
First, investors are loss averse. Second, even investors with long horizons
evaluate their portfolios frequently. Stocks are volatile, so the more often
their value is checked, the more often it shows a loss, and loss aversion makes
each observed loss painful. Using simulations based on historical returns and
the prospect theory parameters of @tversky1992, they found that the size of the
equity premium is consistent with those parameters if investors evaluate their
portfolios annually. The idea echoes a famous anecdote, discussed by
@benartzi1999, in which a colleague of Paul Samuelson declined a single
favourable bet but said he would accept a hundred of them.

Figure \@ref(fig:pt-fig-mla) reproduces the logic in a stylised simulation. It
asks how large an equity premium is needed for a loss-averse investor to be
indifferent between stocks and a riskless bond when gains and losses are
evaluated over horizons from one month to ten years. Table
\@ref(tab:pt-tab-lossprob) shows the reason: the probability of observing a
loss falls steeply as the evaluation period lengthens.

```{r pt-fig-mla, fig.cap = "Stylised simulation of myopic loss aversion. For each evaluation horizon, the curve shows the annual equity premium at which a loss-averse investor with a piecewise-linear value function is indifferent between stocks and a riskless bond. Shorter horizons reveal more losses and require larger premiums. Stylised assumptions: lognormal stock returns with 20% annual volatility, a 1% riskless rate, no probability weighting. This is not the calibration of Benartzi and Thaler (1995).", fig.height = 4.3}
set.seed(1995)
z <- rnorm(200000)
sigma <- 0.20; rf <- 0.01
req_premium <- function(h, lam) {
  t <- h / 12
  bond <- exp(rf * t) - 1                                 # sure gain from the bond
  gap <- function(mu) {
    R <- exp((mu - sigma^2 / 2) * t + sigma * sqrt(t) * z) - 1
    mean(ifelse(R >= 0, R, lam * R)) - bond               # prospect value of stocks minus bonds
  }
  uniroot(gap, c(rf - 0.05, rf + 2))$root - rf
}
mla <- expand.grid(h = c(1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, 60, 120), lambda = c(1.5, 2.25, 3)) |>
  mutate(premium = mapply(req_premium, h, lambda),
         lab = factor(paste0("lambda = ", lambda), levels = paste0("lambda = ", c(1.5, 2.25, 3))))
ggplot(mla, aes(h, premium, colour = lab)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 12, linetype = "dotted", colour = ink[["secondary"]]) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 13, y = max(mla$premium) * 0.9, hjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = ink[["secondary"]],
           label = "Annual evaluation") +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 3, 6, 12, 24, 36, 60, 120),
                labels = c("1 mo", "3 mo", "6 mo", "1 yr", "2 yr", "3 yr", "5 yr", "10 yr")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(pal[["blue"]], pal[["orange"]], pal[["aqua"]])) +
  labs(x = "Evaluation horizon (log scale)", y = "Equity premium needed for indifference", colour = NULL,
       title = "The more often you look, the more premium you need",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (200,000 draws, set.seed(1995)). Illustrative, not empirical estimates.")
```

```{r pt-tab-lossprob}
horiz <- c(`1 day` = 1 / 252, `1 month` = 1 / 12, `1 quarter` = 1 / 4, `1 year` = 1,
           `5 years` = 5, `10 years` = 10, `20 years` = 20)
mu_s <- 0.07                                             # stylised expected return
data.frame(Horizon = names(horiz),
           `Probability of a loss` = scales::percent(
             pnorm(0, (mu_s - 0.2^2 / 2) * horiz, 0.2 * sqrt(horiz)), accuracy = 1),
           check.names = FALSE) |>
  book_table(caption = "Stylised probability that a stock portfolio shows a nominal loss over different evaluation horizons (lognormal returns, 7% expected annual return, 20% volatility). Illustrative values, not historical estimates.",
             full_width = FALSE)
```

### Experimental evidence

The theory makes a sharp, testable prediction: holding the investment
opportunity constant, people who receive feedback and make decisions more
frequently should take *less* risk. Table \@ref(tab:pt-tab-mla-evidence)
summarises the key tests.

```{r pt-tab-mla-evidence}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Study, ~Design, ~Finding,
  "Gneezy & Potters (1997)", "Repeated bets on a favourable lottery, with outcomes evaluated each round or in blocks of rounds", "The more frequently returns were evaluated, the less participants bet",
  "Thaler, Tversky, Kahneman & Schwartz (1997)", "Allocation between a risky and a safe fund, learned from experience, with feedback at different frequencies", "Investors with the most frequent feedback took the least risk and earned the least. Eliminating losses increased risk taking",
  "Haigh & List (2005)", "Gneezy-Potters design with professional futures and options traders and students", "Traders displayed myopic loss aversion to a greater extent than students",
  "Benartzi & Thaler (1999)", "Retirement allocation with one-year versus long-run return distributions", "Showing the long-run distribution increased allocations to stocks"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Experimental tests of myopic loss aversion.")
```

The professional trader result is especially important because it contradicts
the common presumption that market experience eliminates behavioural
anomalies. @haigh2005 expected traders to show less myopic loss aversion than
students. They found more. Asset pricing models have since incorporated these
ideas more formally. @barberis2001 embedded loss aversion over financial wealth
fluctuations, with a reference point that depends on prior gains and losses,
into an equilibrium model that generates a high equity premium and volatile,
predictable returns. @barberis2006 argued that **narrow framing**, evaluating a
gamble in isolation from other risks, is needed to explain why people reject
small independent gambles and why many households do not hold stocks at all.

::: {.business-case}
**Investor feedback and platform design.** Myopic loss aversion implies that
the *frequency and format* of portfolio feedback is a design variable with
consequences for investor welfare. Retirement plan statements that display
long-horizon return distributions, apps that default to showing annual rather
than daily performance, and communications that aggregate accounts rather than
reporting each fund separately all lengthen the effective evaluation period.
**Illustrative scenario:** a robo-advisor testing two dashboards, one showing
daily changes in red and green and one showing progress toward a retirement
goal updated quarterly, would expect the second to produce fewer panic sales
after market declines and higher equity allocations, consistent with
@gneezy1997 and @thaler1997. The ethical question is whether hiding short-run
volatility serves investors or simply keeps assets under management.
:::

::: {.try-it}
Use the simulation code behind Figure \@ref(fig:pt-fig-mla) (change `sigma`,
`rf`, or the `lambda` values) to find the evaluation horizon at which a
loss-averse investor with $\lambda = 2$ would hold stocks at an annual premium
of 4%. How does the answer change if volatility is 15% rather than 20%?
:::

## Disposition Effect {#disposition-effect}

::: {.theory-card}
**Core claim.** Investors are more likely to sell assets that have risen in
value since purchase than assets that have fallen, holding losers too long and
selling winners too early.

**Origins.** Finance. Named by @shefrin1985, documented in brokerage data by
@odean1998, in housing by @genesove2001, and in the laboratory by @weber1998.

**Level of analysis.** Individual investors and property owners, with
implications for trading volume, price momentum, and real estate markets.

**Key constructs.** Purchase price as reference point, realized versus paper
gains and losses, proportion of gains realized (PGR), proportion of losses
realized (PLR), realization utility, regret.

**Boundary conditions.** Weaker among more experienced and sophisticated
investors, and reversed in contexts with strong tax incentives to realize
losses. Its link to prospect theory's value function is debated.

**Related theories.** [Loss aversion](#loss-aversion),
[Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting)),
[Escalation of commitment](#escalation-of-commitment) (Section \@ref(escalation-of-commitment)),
[Behavioral finance](#behavioral-finance) (Section \@ref(behavioral-finance)).
:::

### Origins and core logic

@shefrin1985 coined the term **disposition effect** and proposed an
explanation combining four elements: prospect theory (with the purchase price as
reference point), mental accounting (each stock held in its own account),
regret aversion (realizing a loss confirms a mistake), and self-control
(investors may need rules to overcome the reluctance to sell losers). The
prospect theory logic is that a stock trading above its purchase price is in
the concave, risk-averse region of the value function, which encourages locking
in the gain, while a stock trading below its purchase price is in the convex,
risk-seeking region, which encourages holding on in the hope of breaking even.

### Evidence

@odean1998 developed the standard empirical test using the trading records of
10,000 accounts at a large discount brokerage. On each day an investor sold
any stock, every stock in the portfolio was classified as a realized gain, a
paper (unrealized) gain, a realized loss, or a paper loss. The **proportion of
gains realized**, PGR, is the number of realized gains divided by realized plus
paper gains. The **proportion of losses realized**, PLR, is defined analogously.
Odean found that investors realized gains at a much higher rate than losses,
that the pattern was not explained by portfolio rebalancing or by the higher
trading costs of low-priced stocks, and that it was not justified by subsequent
performance: the winners investors sold went on to outperform the losers they
kept. The code below implements the PGR and PLR calculation for any
position-level dataset and applies it to simulated data.

```{r pt-pgr, echo = TRUE}
# PGR and PLR from position-level data (Odean, 1998).
# d: one row per position held on a day on which the investor sold something,
#    with logical columns `gain` (price above purchase price) and `sold`.
pgr_plr <- function(d) {
  rg <- sum(d$gain & d$sold)
  pg <- sum(d$gain & !d$sold)
  rl <- sum(!d$gain & d$sold)
  pl <- sum(!d$gain & !d$sold)
  pgr <- rg / (rg + pg)
  plr <- rl / (rl + pl)
  se <- sqrt(pgr * (1 - pgr) / (rg + pg) + plr * (1 - plr) / (rl + pl))
  data.frame(PGR = pgr, PLR = plr, Difference = pgr - plr, `t statistic` = (pgr - plr) / se,
             check.names = FALSE)
}

# Simulated (illustrative) investors: selling propensity rises with the size of
# the unrealized return in either direction and jumps just above zero.
set.seed(1998)
sim <- data.frame(investor = rep(1:400, each = 8 * 30),
                  day = rep(rep(1:30, each = 8), 400),
                  ret = rnorm(400 * 8 * 30, 0.02, 0.25))
sim$gain <- sim$ret > 0
sim$sold <- runif(nrow(sim)) < plogis(-2.8 + 0.6 * sim$gain + 2.5 * abs(sim$ret))
sale_days <- unique(sim[sim$sold, c("investor", "day")])
sim_sd <- merge(sim, sale_days)                     # keep only days with a sale
round(pgr_plr(sim_sd), 3)
```

Figure \@ref(fig:pt-fig-disposition) shows the stylised disposition effect in simulated trading data.

```{r pt-fig-disposition, fig.cap = "Stylised disposition effect in simulated trading data. The probability of selling a position on a sale day is plotted against its unrealized return since purchase. Selling rises with the size of the return in both directions and jumps at zero, so the proportion of gains realized (PGR) exceeds the proportion of losses realized (PLR). Illustrative simulation, not empirical data.", fig.height = 4}
binned <- sim_sd |>
  mutate(bin = cut(ret, breaks = seq(-0.6, 0.6, by = 0.05))) |>
  filter(!is.na(bin)) |>
  group_by(bin, gain) |>
  summarise(rate = mean(sold), mid = mean(ret), n = n()) |>
  filter(n >= 50) |>
  mutate(side = ifelse(gain, "Paper gain", "Paper loss"))
rates <- pgr_plr(sim_sd)
ggplot(binned, aes(mid, rate, colour = side)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = ink[["muted"]], linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  annotate("text", x = -0.55, y = max(binned$rate) * 0.95, hjust = 0, size = 3.3, colour = ink[["primary"]],
           label = sprintf("PGR = %.2f\nPLR = %.2f", rates$PGR, rates$PLR)) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Paper gain` = pal[["blue"]], `Paper loss` = pal[["orange"]])) +
  labs(x = "Unrealized return since purchase", y = "Probability of selling on a sale day", colour = NULL,
       title = "Winners are sold more readily than losers",
       caption = "Stylised simulation (400 investors, set.seed(1998)). Not empirical data.")
```

The effect is not confined to stock markets. @genesove2001 found that Boston
condominium owners facing nominal losses in the 1990s set asking prices higher
by 25-35% of the difference between the property's expected selling price and
their original purchase price, achieved higher selling prices by 3-18% of that
difference, and sold much more slowly than other sellers. The list price
effects were about twice as large for owner-occupants as for investors but held
for both. In a controlled experimental market where the expected returns of
assets were known, @weber1998 also found that participants sold more winners
than losers.

::: {.debate}
**Is the disposition effect really prospect theory?** The textbook explanation
has been challenged on theoretical and empirical grounds. @barberis2009 modelled
a prospect-theory investor carefully and found that when preferences are
defined over annual gains and losses, the model often predicts the *opposite* of
the disposition effect. A loss-averse investor buys a stock only if its
expected return is high. After a gain she moves away from the kink in the value
function and is willing to hold more, while after a loss she moves toward the
kink, where loss aversion bites hardest, and reduces her position. The
disposition effect emerges more reliably if utility is derived from *realizing*
gains and losses, a preference that @barberis2009 call **realization utility**.
@kaustia2010 showed that the propensity to sell jumps at a zero return but is
approximately constant over a wide range of losses and constant or increasing
over gains, a pattern hard to reconcile with the curvature of the value
function.
@bendavid2012 found that selling is V-shaped in past returns: investors are more
likely to sell large winners *and* large losers than small ones, which suggests
belief-based trading rather than a preference for realizing gains.
@imas2016 added a twist: after a *realized* loss people take less risk, but
after a *paper* loss they take more, so the act of realization itself changes
the reference point. The consensus is that the disposition effect is a robust
empirical regularity whose cause is more likely realization utility, regret, or
beliefs than the S-shaped value function alone.
:::

Table \@ref(tab:pt-tab-disposition) presents the explanations for the disposition effect.

```{r pt-tab-disposition}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Explanation, ~`Core idea`, ~`Key evidence or source`,
  "Prospect theory value function", "Concavity above and convexity below the purchase price", "Shefrin & Statman (1985), but see Barberis & Xiong (2009)",
  "Realization utility", "Investors derive utility from the act of realizing a gain or loss", "Barberis & Xiong (2009)",
  "Regret and self-justification", "Selling a loser confirms a mistake", "Shefrin & Statman (1985)",
  "Beliefs in mean reversion", "Investors expect losers to rebound and winners to fall back", "Odean (1998) rules out several rational motives, Ben-David & Hirshleifer (2012)",
  "Break-even seeking", "Paper losses invite risk taking to get back to the reference point", "Thaler & Johnson (1990), Imas (2016)",
  "Tax considerations", "Realizing losses reduces tax liability", "Predicts the opposite pattern, so it cannot explain the effect"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Explanations for the disposition effect.")
```

::: {.business-case}
**Brokerage and wealth-management practice.** The disposition effect has
practical consequences for retail investors, who sell winners that keep
winning and hold losers that keep losing, and for the firms that serve them.
Practices that weaken the effect include automatic rebalancing rules, pre-set
stop-loss and take-profit rules decided before positions move, year-round
tax-loss harvesting that reframes a realized loss as a tax gain, and statements
that report portfolio-level rather than position-level returns, which makes the
purchase price of each holding less salient. In real estate, agents can use
the evidence of @genesove2001 to anticipate that sellers facing nominal losses
will over-price and stay on the market longer, and price-setting conversations
can shift the reference point from the purchase price to recent comparable
sales.
:::

## Further Applications {#prospect-theory-applications}

Few theories have travelled as far as prospect theory. Table
\@ref(tab:pt-tab-applications) maps its components to application domains,
and the subsections that follow discuss the most important ones for business
and policy. Each application relies on a different part of the theory, which is
worth keeping in mind: evidence for one component (for example, probability
weighting in lottery markets) is not evidence for another (for example, loss
aversion in labour supply).

```{r pt-tab-applications}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Domain, ~`Component of the theory`, ~`Signature prediction`, ~`Illustrative evidence`,
  "Pricing", "Reference dependence, loss aversion", "Surcharges and price increases hurt more than equivalent discounts and decreases help", "Thaler (1980), Hardie et al. (1993)",
  "Promotions and messaging", "Framing, loss aversion", "Loss-framed messages can motivate more than gain-framed ones", "Ganzach & Karsahi (1995)",
  "Insurance", "Probability weighting, loss aversion", "Over-insurance of modest risks, preference for low deductibles", "Johnson et al. (1993), Sydnor (2010)",
  "Lotteries and skewed assets", "Overweighting of small probabilities", "Demand for and overpricing of lottery-like payoffs", "Barberis & Huang (2008)",
  "Asset pricing", "Myopic loss aversion, narrow framing", "High equity premium, non-participation", "Benartzi & Thaler (1995), Barberis et al. (2001)",
  "Trading", "Purchase price as reference point", "Disposition effect", "Odean (1998), Genesove & Mayer (2001)",
  "Labour and effort", "Expectations and goals as reference points", "Bunching at targets, effort responds to expectations", "Abeler et al. (2011), Allen et al. (2017)",
  "Tax compliance", "Loss aversion around a zero balance due", "More avoidance when a payment is owed than when a refund is due", "Engström et al. (2015), Rees-Jones (2018)",
  "Health and energy", "Goal framing, loss-framed incentives", "Deposit contracts and loss-framed incentives can outperform equivalent rewards", "Patel et al. (2016), Halpern et al. (2015)",
  "Negotiation and politics", "Reference dependence, reflection effect", "Loss frames make negotiators tougher and leaders more risk seeking", "Neale & Bazerman (1985), Levy (1992)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Prospect theory applications by domain.")
```

### Pricing and reference prices

The idea that customers code prices relative to a reference point is the most
direct business application of the theory. @thaler1980 noted that the credit
card industry preferred that any price difference between card and cash
payments be described as a "cash discount" rather than a "credit card
surcharge", anticipating that a surcharge would be coded as a loss. Reference
prices also govern perceptions of fairness: customers accept price increases
that pass on higher costs but regard increases that exploit a surge in demand as
unfair, because the previous price acts as a reference transaction
[@kahneman1986]. In scanner-panel data, @hardie1993 modelled brand choice with
reference-dependent utility and found evidence of loss aversion with respect to
the reference brand's price and quality: consumers were more responsive to
being worse off than to being better off relative to the brand they had last
bought. @kalyanaram1995 summarized the empirical generalizations of reference
price research, beginning with the finding that reference prices significantly
affect demand.

::: {.business-case}
**Framing price differences.** The same price structure can be presented as a
surcharge (the base price is the low price, and some customers pay extra) or as
a discount (the base price is the high price, and some customers pay less).
Prospect theory predicts that customers who end up paying the higher price will
feel worse under the surcharge frame, and customers who pay the lower price will
feel only mildly better under the discount frame. Airlines, utilities, and
payment providers face this choice every time they differentiate prices by
channel, time, or payment method. Combined with mental accounting, the theory
also predicts that many small fees, each coded as a separate loss, will feel
worse than one all-inclusive price ([Mental accounting](#mental-accounting) (Section \@ref(mental-accounting))).
The managerial implication is not always to choose the discount frame: a
surcharge may be the more effective way to steer customers toward a cheaper
channel precisely because it is more aversive, but it carries reputational
costs that the discount frame avoids.
:::

### Promotions and marketing messages

Loss framing is a standard tool in promotional copy ("Don't miss out",
"You are losing \$X a month"). The evidence is supportive but more nuanced than
practitioners assume. In a field experiment with credit card holders,
@ganzach1995 found that a message emphasizing what customers lose by not using
their card produced more subsequent card use than a message emphasizing what
they gain by using it. Goal-framing effects of this kind are, however,
distinct from risky-choice framing and attribute framing, and they vary in size
and even direction across settings [@levin1998]. Firms should treat loss
framing as a hypothesis to test in controlled experiments.

### Insurance, lotteries, and skewed assets

Insurance and lotteries are where probability weighting does most of its work.
Overweighting of small probabilities makes people willing to pay well above
expected value both to eliminate a small chance of loss (insurance) and to buy a
small chance of a large gain (lotteries), the two "low probability" cells of
the fourfold pattern. Reviewing three decades of applications in economics,
@barberis2013 highlighted insurance and finance as domains in which the theory
helps to explain facts that are otherwise hard to account for. @sydnor2010
studied deductible choices in home insurance and found that most customers
chose low deductibles despite premiums far above the expected value of the
additional coverage, a level of risk aversion over modest stakes that a standard
expected-utility model can fit only with implausible parameters. In financial
markets, @barberis2008 showed that investors with cumulative prospect theory
preferences overvalue securities with positively skewed, lottery-like returns,
which can make such securities earn low average returns, and @barberis2016
found that stocks whose past return distributions are more attractive under
prospect theory tend to have lower subsequent returns.

::: {.business-case}
**Insurance deductibles and extended warranties.** Low deductibles, extended
warranties, and add-on protection plans sell well even when their price is many
times the expected cost of the risk they cover [@sydnor2010]. Prospect theory
offers two reasons. Small probabilities of loss are overweighted, and paying a
deductible after a claim is coded as an additional, salient loss on top of the
damage itself. Insurers can use this insight responsibly, for example by
offering a low-deductible option alongside clear information on expected claim
costs, or exploitatively, by pricing low-deductible options far above cost.
Regulators and consumer advocates increasingly treat the second as a
consumer-protection issue.
:::

### Labour and tax compliance

Reference points shape how people respond to taxes. In Sweden, taxpayers
receive a preliminary statement showing whether they owe money or are due a
refund. Using data on 3.6 million Swedish taxpayers and a regression kink and
discontinuity design, @engstrom2015 found strong causal effects of a
preliminary deficit on the probability of claiming deductions, and concluded
that calibrating withholding so that most taxpayers receive refunds would
increase compliance. In US tax returns, @reesjones2018 estimated that taxpayers
facing a payment on tax day reduce their tax liability by \$34 more than
taxpayers owed a refund. In both studies, the reference point is a zero balance
due, and owing money is coded as a loss. Labour-market applications, including
effort provision, daily labour supply, and job search, are discussed in
[Reference-dependent preferences](#reference-dependent-preferences).

### Sports

Sport provides unusually clean tests because outcomes are precisely measured
and reference points are institutionally defined: par in golf [@pope2011],
round-number finishing times in marathons [@allen2017], and betting lines in
football [@card2011]. Sports settings also show that reference dependence
survives expertise, high stakes, and competition, which answers the common
objection that behavioural anomalies disappear among experienced professionals
operating in markets.

### Public policy and health messaging

@rothman1997 proposed an influential refinement of goal framing for health
communication. Behaviours that *prevent* illness (sunscreen, exercise) are
perceived as low risk, so gain-framed messages should be more persuasive.
Behaviours that *detect* illness (screening) carry the risk of an unwelcome
discovery, so loss-framed messages should be more persuasive, by analogy with
the risk seeking that prospect theory predicts in the loss domain. Early
evidence was encouraging: women who read pamphlets emphasizing the negative
consequences of *not* performing breast self-examination showed more favourable
attitudes and behaviour than those who read pamphlets emphasizing the benefits
of performing it [@meyerowitz1987]. Meta-analytic evidence is more sobering:
across disease-prevention studies, the average difference between gain-framed
and loss-framed messages is small [@okeefe2007].

Loss aversion has had more consistent success in the design of *incentives*
than of messages. In a randomized trial with overweight and obese adults,
@patel2016 compared financial incentives for meeting a daily step goal that were
framed as gains, as lotteries, or as losses (money allocated in advance and
taken away for each day the goal was missed). Only the loss-framed incentive
increased goal attainment significantly relative to control. In a large trial
of smoking-cessation programmes, @halpern2015 found that deposit contracts, in
which participants put their own money at risk, were accepted by fewer people
than reward programmes, but were more effective among those who accepted them,
illustrating the trade-off between the motivational power of loss-based
incentives and their unattractiveness at enrolment. @volpp2008 found that both
deposit contracts and lottery-based incentives produced more weight loss than
a control condition during a weight-loss intervention.

::: {.business-case}
**Loss-framed energy and health messages.** In a classic quasi-experiment,
home energy auditors were trained to communicate their findings
vividly and to frame the potential savings as money the household was *losing*
through leaks and poor insulation. Homeowners who received these audits were
more likely to apply for retrofit programmes than homeowners who received
standard audits [@gonzales1988]. Utilities and health insurers have since used
similar framing alongside other behavioural levers such as social comparisons
([Social norms](#social-norms) (Section \@ref(social-norms))), and loss-framed incentive designs such as
pre-funded wellness accounts draw directly on @patel2016. The lesson from the
meta-analytic evidence [@okeefe2007] is that loss frames are not a universal
improvement: they work best when the behaviour involves risk or uncertainty and
when the reference point is clear to the audience.
:::

### Negotiation and politics

In a negotiation, what one side gives up is coded as a loss and what it
receives as a gain, so concessions loom larger to the conceder than to the
recipient. @neale1985 showed that framing changes bargaining: negotiators
instructed to think about their outcomes as gains were more concessionary and
completed more transactions than negotiators instructed to think about them as
losses. In international relations, @levy1992 argued that prospect theory
explains why states and leaders accept large risks to avoid losses (for example,
to recover lost territory or status) that they would not accept to make
equivalent gains, while noting the analytical difficulty of identifying the
reference point of a state.

::: {.research-toolkit}
**Bringing prospect theory to a new domain.**

- **Specify the component.** State whether the prediction rests on reference
  dependence, loss aversion, diminishing sensitivity, or probability weighting.
- **Identify the reference point ex ante.** Use institutional features (par,
  purchase price, zero balance due, quota) or measured expectations.
- **Find a discontinuity.** Reference points create kinks and notches.
  Bunching and regression discontinuity designs exploit them.
- **Rule out alternatives.** Inertia, attention, transaction costs, beliefs,
  and the range of outcomes can all mimic loss aversion.
- **Sample hypothesis.** *H1.* Customers who receive a loss-framed renewal
  reminder ("You will lose your saved settings") will renew at a higher rate
  than customers who receive an equivalent gain-framed reminder, and the effect
  will be larger among customers with higher usage (a stronger sense of
  ownership).
:::

## Replication and Robustness {#prospect-theory-replication}

Prospect theory is built on demonstrations that are cheap to run, which makes
it unusually easy to test whether its foundations replicate. The answer is
encouraging. @ruggeri2020 repeated the original 1979 choice problems with 4,098
participants in 19 countries and 13 languages, adjusting only the currency and
amounts to local conditions and requiring every participant to answer every
item. The results replicated for 94% of items, with some attenuation of effect
sizes, and 12 of 13 theoretical contrasts replicated, with complete replication
in some countries. The authors also documented meaningful heterogeneity between
countries and within individuals. The framing effect in the "Asian disease"
problem [@tversky1981] was among the effects that replicated in the first Many
Labs project [@klein2014].

The picture is more mixed for the theory's *extensions* and *field
applications*. Table \@ref(tab:pt-tab-replication) summarises the state of the
evidence as of this writing.

```{r pt-tab-replication}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Claim, ~Status, ~`Evidence`,
  "Certainty, reflection, and isolation effects in described lotteries", "Replicates", "Ruggeri et al. (2020): 94% of items and 12 of 13 contrasts, with some attenuation",
  "Risky-choice framing (Asian disease)", "Replicates", "Many Labs 1 (Klein et al., 2014)",
  "Loss aversion on average", "Replicates, smaller than 2.25", "Meta-analytic mean 1.955 (Brown et al., 2024)",
  "Loss aversion as a universal constant", "Does not hold", "Context and range effects, small stakes, exchange goods (Walasek & Stewart, 2015, Harinck et al., 2007, Novemsky & Kahneman, 2005)",
  "Overweighting of rare events", "Holds for description, often reverses for experience", "Hertwig et al. (2004)",
  "Expectations as reference points", "Mixed", "Abeler et al. (2011) versus Gneezy et al. (2017) and Heffetz & List (2014)",
  "Daily income targeting by taxi drivers", "Contested", "Camerer et al. (1997) versus Farber (2008, 2015), Thakral & Tô (2021)",
  "Myopic loss aversion", "Replicates in experiments, including with professionals", "Gneezy & Potters (1997), Haigh & List (2005)",
  "Disposition effect as an empirical regularity", "Robust", "Odean (1998), Genesove & Mayer (2001), Weber & Camerer (1998)",
  "Disposition effect caused by the S-shaped value function", "Doubtful", "Barberis & Xiong (2009), Kaustia (2010), Ben-David & Hirshleifer (2012)",
  "Reference dependence in high-stakes field settings", "Robust", "Pope & Schweitzer (2011), Allen et al. (2017), Card & Dahl (2011)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "What replicates and what does not: the state of the evidence on prospect theory.")
```

Three lessons emerge. First, the *qualitative* patterns that motivated prospect
theory are among the most reliable findings in the behavioural sciences.
Second, *quantitative* parameters, especially the loss aversion coefficient,
vary with people, tasks, and contexts, so a single "true" value should not be
imported uncritically into applied models. Third, the theory's empirical
success in a new domain depends on how well the reference point is specified,
which is a modelling choice rather than a prediction of the theory itself
[@barberis2013; @odonoghue2018].

::: {.pitfall}
**Importing parameter values without checking the context.** Simulations and
structural models often plug in $\alpha = 0.88$, $\lambda = 2.25$, and
$\gamma = 0.61$ as if they were universal constants. They are median estimates
from one study of described lotteries. When results depend on these values,
report sensitivity analyses over plausible ranges, for example $\lambda$ from
about 1.5 to 2.5, and prefer estimates from populations and tasks similar to
the application.
:::

## Chapter Summary {#prospect-theory-summary}

::: {.key-takeaways}
- **Expected utility theory** remains the normative benchmark, but the Allais
  and Ellsberg paradoxes and Rabin's calibration theorem show that it cannot
  describe how people actually evaluate risk, especially over modest stakes
  [@allais1953; @ellsberg1961; @rabin2000].
- **Prospect theory** replaces final wealth with gains and losses relative to a
  reference point, and combines a value function (diminishing sensitivity and
  loss aversion) with decision weights (overweighting of small probabilities)
  [@kahneman1979].
- **Cumulative prospect theory** applies weights to cumulative probabilities,
  preserving dominance and generating the fourfold pattern of risk attitudes.
  Its median parameters, $\alpha = \beta = 0.88$, $\lambda = 2.25$,
  $\gamma = 0.61$, and $\delta = 0.69$, are useful defaults, not constants
  [@tversky1992].
- **Loss aversion** is real on average, with a meta-analytic mean coefficient
  near 2, but it is moderated by stakes, goods, experience, and the range of
  outcomes [@brown2024; @mrkva2020; @walasek2015].
- **Reference points** can be the status quo, expectations, goals, or salient
  numbers. Expectation-based models discipline the choice but have mixed
  experimental support [@koszegi2006; @abeler2011; @gneezy2017].
- **Status quo bias**, **myopic loss aversion**, and the **disposition effect**
  are the theory's most consequential applications, with large effects on
  retirement saving, asset prices, and trading [@madrian2001; @benartzi1995;
  @odean1998].
- The original choice patterns **replicate** across 19 countries
  [@ruggeri2020]. The theory's weakest point is not its foundations but the
  specification of the reference point in each new application.
:::

Table \@ref(tab:pt-tab-summary) presents the comparison of expected utility, prospect theory, cumulative prospect theory, and expectation-based reference-dependent preferences.

```{r pt-tab-summary}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Feature, ~`Expected utility`, ~`Prospect theory (1979)`, ~`Cumulative prospect theory (1992)`, ~`Expectation-based reference dependence (2006)`,
  "Carriers of value", "Final wealth", "Gains and losses", "Gains and losses", "Consumption plus gains and losses",
  "Reference point", "None", "Usually the status quo, unspecified", "Usually the status quo, unspecified", "Recent rational expectations (stochastic)",
  "Risk attitude from", "Curvature of utility", "Value function and decision weights", "Value function and rank-dependent weights", "Consumption utility and gain-loss utility",
  "Probability treatment", "Linear", "Decision weights on individual probabilities", "Weights on cumulative probabilities", "Usually linear",
  "Loss aversion", "No", "Yes", "Yes (lambda)", "Yes (lambda), relative to expectations",
  "Stochastic dominance", "Satisfied", "Can be violated", "Satisfied", "Satisfied in standard applications",
  "Signature prediction", "Consistent preferences across common consequences", "Certainty, reflection, isolation effects", "Fourfold pattern of risk attitudes", "Surprises, not outcomes, drive gain-loss feelings",
  "Key source", "von Neumann & Morgenstern (1944)", "Kahneman & Tversky (1979)", "Tversky & Kahneman (1992)", "Kőszegi & Rabin (2006)"
) |>
  book_table(caption = "Comparison of expected utility, prospect theory, cumulative prospect theory, and expectation-based reference-dependent preferences.")
```

## Discussion Questions {#prospect-theory-questions}

1. Rabin's calibration theorem is sometimes described as the strongest argument
   for prospect theory. Explain the theorem in your own words. Does it show that
   expected utility is wrong, or only that wealth is the wrong argument of the
   utility function?
2. Choose a pricing decision in a firm you know (a price increase, a new fee, a
   change in subscription terms). Identify at least three candidate reference
   points customers could use, and design a field experiment that would reveal
   which one drives their response.
3. The debate over loss aversion has moved from *whether* losses loom larger
   than gains to *when* and *for whom*. Propose a study that would distinguish
   loss aversion from inertia in a setting of your choice.
4. Using Figure \@ref(fig:pt-fig-mla) and the evidence on myopic loss aversion,
   argue for or against a regulation that would require retirement plan
   providers to show long-horizon return distributions by default. Whose
   interests would such a rule serve?
5. The disposition effect is robust, but its cause is debated. What data from a
   brokerage platform would allow you to distinguish realization utility,
   beliefs in mean reversion, and the S-shaped value function as explanations?
6. Loss-framed incentives (deposit contracts, claw-back bonuses) can be more
   effective than equivalent rewards but are less attractive at enrolment and
   can feel unfair. Under what conditions should an employer or health insurer
   use them?

## Further Reading {#prospect-theory-reading}

- @kahneman1979: the original paper. Read the choice problems first, then the
  model, and notice how much of later research is foreshadowed in the
  discussion of editing.
- @tversky1992: the cumulative version, with the parameter estimates that
  became the field's defaults.
- @wakker2010: the definitive technical treatment of prospect theory for risk
  and ambiguity, with careful attention to measurement.
- @barberis2013: an accessible assessment of thirty years of applications in
  economics, especially finance and insurance.
- @odonoghue2018: a rigorous handbook review of reference-dependent
  preferences, including the Kőszegi-Rabin model and the field evidence.
- @brown2024: the most comprehensive meta-analysis of loss aversion estimates.
  Pair it with @gal2018 and @mrkva2020 for the debate.
- @ruggeri2020: a multinational replication of the original problems and a
  model of how to test a classic finding at scale.
- @dellavigna2009: a survey of field evidence in psychology and economics,
  with an extensive section on reference dependence.
